abstract.t: This document defines the mapping of the RESTful Provisioning Protocol (RPP) to the HTTP protocol. RPP is used for the provisioning and management of objects in a shared database. The RPP data model, consisting of Data Objects and their operations, is defined in . This document specifies how those Data Objects and operations are mapped to HTTP resources, methods, header fields, and status codes, and how RPP servers are discovered. The mapping is independent of the data format used to represent RPP messages.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: This document describes an Application Programming Interface (API) based on HTTP as defined in and the principles of . Conforming to the REST constraints is generally referred to as being "RESTful". Hence the API is dubbed: "RESTful Provisioning Protocol" or "RPP" for short.
The RPP API is designed to be used for the provisioning and management of objects in a shared database, such as domain names and their name servers (hosts).

The RPP data model, including the Data Objects, their data elements, and the operations defined on them, is specified independently of any protocol in . This document is the mapping of that data model to HTTP. It defines how the URL, HTTP method, header fields, and HTTP status code for each operation are derived from the Data Object definitions, as well as bootstrapping, discovery, versioning, media type negotiation, error reporting, and authentication.

This document does not define a data format. The representation of RPP messages in a specific data format, for example JSON, is defined in a separate representation specification that registers an RPP media type.
TODO Rename this document to better reflect its role as the HTTP mapping of the RPP data model.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: In this document the following terminology is used.
REST - Representational State Transfer (). An architectural style.
RESTful - A RESTful web service is a web service or API implemented using HTTP and the principles of .
RESTful Provisioning Protocol or RPP - The protocol described in this document.
URL - A Uniform Resource Locator as defined in .
Resource - An object having a type, data, and possible relationship to other resources, identified by a URL.
RPP client - An HTTP user agent performing an RPP request
RPP server - An HTTP server responsible for processing requests and returning results in any supported media type.
JWT - JSON Web Token as defined in .
RPP media type - A media type, defined in a representation specification, that carries RPP messages in a specific data format.

Label Generation Ruleset (LGR) - A set of rules defining the valid labels for a registry, including the permitted repertoire, contextual rules, and, where applicable, variant mappings. Also historically known as IDN tables .

section.name: Conventions Used in This Document
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

All example requests assume an RPP server is available on the standard HTTPS port on host rpp.example. An authorisation token has been provided by an out-of-band process and is used by the client to authenticate each request.

section.name: Notational Conventions
section.t: This document uses the following terminology from to specify syntax and parsing: Item, String, and Integer.

This document does not mandate any particular authority (host and port) or path prefix for an RPP server. The rpp.example authority and the /rpp path prefix used throughout the examples in this document are purely illustrative. All URLs used in examples are presumed to be relative to the value defined for the base_url field of the well-known discovery document.

section.name: Mapping to EPP
section.t: RPP is designed as an independent protocol and does not require an EPP server. RPP concepts such as transaction identifiers, result codes, and object attributes are defined in their own right and serve RPP purposes regardless of whether an EPP backend is present. However, compatibility with EPP is preserved to a great extent. Implementers with no prior EPP experience are able to implement RPP based solely on this specification.

Some RPP concepts are functionally similar to EPP concepts, but they are not directly derived from EPP and MAY have different semantics. To avoid confusion, RPP elements SHOULD NOT use an EPP prefix or suffix. For implementers who operate an EPP backend and need to bridge RPP requests to EPP commands, a separate RPP-to-EPP mapping document [TODO REF] is provided. Any extensions to RPP are not covered by that mapping document; the mapping of extension elements MUST be defined in the respective extension specification.

section.name: Header Fields
section.t: HTTP header fields defined by RPP MUST use the RPP- prefix and MUST be defined as Structured Fields , unless the syntax of the field value cannot be expressed as an Item, List or Dictionary. A header field definition that is not a Structured Field MUST state this explicitly. RPP also uses existing standard header fields, such as Link , which do not use the RPP- prefix.

section.name: Request Header Fields
section.t: This document defines the RPP-Cltrid, RPP-Authorization and RPP-Profile request header fields.

ul.li: RPP-Cltrid: A client-assigned transaction identifier. The client MUST include this header field in every request. It serves two independent purposes: as an idempotency key, allowing the server to detect and safely handle duplicate requests, and as an audit-trail identifier, enabling end-to-end correlation of a request across client and server logs. The value MUST be unique per request. The RPP-Cltrid header field's value is an Item of type String.

li.t: RPP-Authorization: The client MAY use this header field to send authorisation information in the format <method> <authorization information>, similar to the Authorization header field defined in . The RPP-Authorization header field is specific for each User Agent and MUST NOT be cached, as recommended by . The <method> indicates the type of authorisation being used. For EPP object authorisation information, for example the authorisation information used for domain names described in , a new authinfo method is defined. The <authorization information> defines the following comma-separated fields:

ul.li: value (REQUIRED): Base64 encoded EPP password-based authorisation information. The content of the value field is case sensitive.

roid (OPTIONAL): A Roid as defined in , , and . The roid is used to identify the object for which the authorisation information is provided. If the roid is not provided, then the server MUST assume that the authorisation information is linked to the object identified by the URL of the request.

section.t: Example request using the RPP-Authorization header field:
section.sourcecode: GET /domainNames/foo.example HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Authorization: authinfo value=TXkgU2VjcmV0IFRva2Vu, roid=REG-123

ul.li: RPP-Profile: The client MUST use this header field to indicate the profile that is used in the request.

section.name: Response Header Fields
section.t: This document defines the RPP-Svtrid, RPP-Cltrid, RPP-Code, RPP-Queue-Size and RPP-Profile response header fields.

ul.li: RPP-Svtrid: A server-assigned transaction identifier. The server MUST include this header field in every response, providing a unique, server-side audit-trail reference for the processed request. Because this header field maps the EPP svTRID element, whose syntax differs from the String type defined in , RPP-Svtrid MUST NOT be defined as a Structured Field.

section.t: Example response including the RPP-Svtrid header field:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

ul.li: RPP-Cltrid: The server MUST echo the client transaction identifier from the request back to the client in this response header field. This allows the client to correlate responses to their originating requests. Because this header field maps the EPP clTRID element, whose syntax differs from the String type defined in , RPP-Cltrid MUST NOT be defined as a Structured Field.

section.t: Example response including the RPP-Cltrid header field:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

li.t: RPP-Code: This header field contains the RPP result code indicating the outcome of the request. This header field MUST be included in all responses and MAY be used by the client for easy access to the result code, without having to parse the HTTP response content. The RPP-Code header field's value is an Item of type String.

RPP-Queue-Size: Returns the number of unacknowledged messages in the client message queue. The server MAY include this header field in all RPP responses. The RPP-Queue-Size header field's value is an Item of type Integer and MUST be greater than or equal to 0.

Link: When a uniform interface operation implicitly creates a process object as a side effect, the server MUST communicate the URL of the created process resource using the Link response header field with the rpp-process relation type. If multiple process objects are created, the server MUST include one Link header field per created process resource, each with rel="rpp-process".

section.t: Example response with the Link header field to indicate the URL of a process object created as a side effect of a domain create request:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Location: https://rpp.example/rpp/domainNames/foo.example Link: <https://rpp.example/rpp/domainNames/foo.example/processes/\ createProcesses/latest>; rel="rpp-process"; process="createProcess"; \ processId="XYZ-12345" RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

ul.li: RPP-Profile: The server MUST use this header field to indicate the profile that is used in the response.

section.name: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
section.t: RPP servers MAY be accessed directly by browser-based clients. To support such clients, RPP servers SHOULD implement Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) as defined in .
When responding to a CORS preflight (OPTIONS) request, the server SHOULD include the following in its response:

ul.li: Access-Control-Allow-Methods: The HTTP methods supported for the requested endpoint.
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: All request header fields defined in this specification in addition to Content-Type and Accept.
Access-Control-Expose-Headers: All request and response header fields defined in this specification.

section.t: The server MUST allow every RPP media type it supports to be used in the Content-Type and Accept header fields of cross-origin requests.

section.name: Redirection
section.t: An RPP server, or an HTTP intermediary, can redirect a request to another URL. Depending on the status code, an HTTP client can change the method of the request when following a redirect, for example from POST to GET, which may break RPP processing. Therefore, as recommended by , this section defines how redirects are handled by RPP.

An RPP server MUST use only the 307 (Temporary Redirect) or 308 (Permanent Redirect) status code ( and ) when redirecting a request, because these status codes do not allow the client to change the request method. A redirect response MUST include a Location header field containing an absolute URL using the https scheme.

An RPP client MAY follow a 307 or 308 redirect response. When following a redirect, the client MUST send the same request content and the same header fields as in the original request, including the RPP-Cltrid header field, so that the redirected request is the same request for the purpose of idempotency. The client MUST NOT send the Authorization and RPP-Authorization header fields to an origin that differs from the origin of the original request, unless the client knows that the target origin is an alias of the origin of the original request, or the client has credentials that are valid for the new target origin. In the latter case the client uses the credentials for the new target origin, which can differ from the credentials used for the original request.
An RPP client MUST NOT follow a response with any other redirection status code, for example because an HTTP intermediary generated it, and MUST treat such a response as a protocol error.

section.name: Problem Detail Responses for Errors
section.t: When an error occurs that prevents processing of the requested action, an RPP server MUST respond using a Problem Detail document detailing what went wrong, or what was not acceptable to the server. The type field MUST be the urn:ietf:params:rpp:error URN. The status field MUST reflect the HTTP status code. The document MUST contain an errors element, as a list of objects detailing individual errors.
This document consists of the following fields:

dl.dd: (required, string) This field MUST always contain the fixed string value urn:ietf:params:rpp:error to indicate that this is an RPP Problem Detail response.
(required, string) A short human-readable description of the Problem Detail type.

(optional, array of error objects) MUST contain objects detailing information about the specific errors that occurred, including optional references to which values in the original request were not acceptable to the server.

section.t: The error object consists of the following fields:

dl.dd: (required, string) This field SHOULD be a URI that identifies the error type. This URI MAY be dereferenceable to obtain human-readable documentation about the error type.
(required, string) This field MUST contain the RPP result code associated with the error.

(optional, list of strings) The JSONPath to the value(s) in the request that caused the error. This field MAY be omitted if no specific value in the request can be identified as the cause of the error.
(required, string) A human-readable detailed description of the error.

section.t: RPP specifications and/or extensions MAY add extension fields to the error object, to convey additional information about the causes of the error. For example, to indicate the account balance on a billing failure, the following Problem Detail response could be used:

Problem Detail response containing multiple errors for a domain create request using an invalid domain name (_$.example), JSONPaths are specified in the error objects to indicate which value in the request caused the error:

section.name: Bootstrapping
section.t: The server MUST provide a mechanism for clients to discover the location of the RPP server, two methods are defined for this purpose, using the IANA registry for RPP servers or using DNS-based bootstrapping. The server MUST provide at least one of these methods, and MAY provide both methods. The client MUST use either the IANA registry for RPP servers or a DNS lookup using an HTTPS resource record as defined in . The client MUST be able to handle the case where the chosen method does not return a valid RPP server location, and MUST be able to use the other method as a fallback to discover the RPP server location.

The format and procedure for adding an RPP server to the IANA registry is defined in the IANA Considerations section below. If the server uses both the IANA registry and DNS-based bootstrapping, then both methods MUST return the same location for the RPP server.

For DNS-based bootstrapping, an RPP server MUST publish an HTTPS resource record in a _rpp child zone for each DNS zone that is managed by the RPP server. The owner name of the HTTPS resource record MUST be the managed zone name itself, prepended with the _rpp. label (i.e., _rpp.<zone>).

If multiple HTTPS resource records are returned, the client MUST process them according to the priority rules defined in . If multiple records have the same SvcPriority, the client SHOULD select one based on local policy.
The client MUST construct the URL for the well-known endpoint of the RPP server as follows, using the TargetName and port SvcParams from the HTTPS resource record:

ul.li: https://<TargetName>:<port>/.well-known/rpp when the port SvcParam is present and not 443
https://<TargetName>/.well-known/rpp when the port SvcParam is absent or is 443

section.t: Example HTTPS resource record for an RPP server for the TLD example running HTTPS on port 443 at rpp.example.:
section.sourcecode: $ORIGIN example. _rpp IN HTTPS 1 rpp.example. alpn=h2,h3
section.t: In this example, the well-known endpoint URL is https://rpp.example/.well-known/rpp.
Example HTTPS resource record for an RPP server using a different TargetName (rpp-svr2.registry.example) and a non-standard port (8443) for the TLD example:
section.sourcecode: $ORIGIN example. _rpp IN HTTPS 1 rpp-svr2.registry.example. alpn=h2,h3 port=8443
section.t: In this example, the well-known endpoint URL is https://rpp-svr2.registry.example:8443/.well-known/rpp.

section.name: Discoverability
section.t: An RPP client MUST be able to discover the capabilities of the RPP server before performing any provisioning operations. The Discovery Data Object defined in MUST be mapped to the well-known endpoint at /.well-known/rpp, and MUST return a representation describing the capabilities of the RPP server. The well-known endpoint MUST be accessible, using the HTTP GET method, without authentication and MUST return the 200 (OK) status code if the request was successful.

section.name: Workflow
section.t: The steps for a typical workflow of provisioning an object using RPP without knowing the location and capabilities of the server are as follows, the first three steps are optional, the client can choose to skip any of these steps if it already has the required information from a previous interaction or configuration.

ol.li: Bootstrap (optional): The client discovers the location of the RPP server by looking up the IANA registry for RPP servers or by performing a DNS HTTPS lookup as defined in .
Discover capabilities (optional): The client retrieves the capabilities of the RPP server by sending a GET request to the well-known endpoint at /.well-known/rpp.
Extract RPP URLs (optional): The client extracts the base URL and endpoint URL templates from the discovery response, and uses this information to construct the URLs for the desired operations.

Perform provisioning operations: The client performs provisioning operations by sending HTTP requests to the appropriate endpoint URLs, using the HTTP method and request content as required by the specific operation.

section.name: Versioning
section.t: RPP operator MAY support more than one version of RPP. The versioning scheme uses the Semantic Versioning format defined in , where major version number is used to indicate breaking changes. In this case of incompatible versions the operator MUST deploy them on distinct base_url and announce them in discovery document.

The client MUST indicate the version of RPP it is using by including an RPP media type with a version parameter in the Accept header field of each request, for example: application/rpp+json; version=1.0. The server MUST include the media type used in the request in its response to the client. The server MUST reject requests using an unsupported version of RPP, and MUST return a 406 (Not Acceptable) status code.
The following additional RPP elements include versioning support:

ul.li: Messages: A request and response message MUST include the version of the RPP API it is compatible with.
Extensions: RPP extensions MUST include the version of the RPP API they are compatible with.
Profiles: RPP profiles MUST include the version of the RPP API they are compatible with.
Media types: RPP media types MUST include the version of the RPP API they are compatible with.
Result codes: RPP result codes may be added by extensions or updates to the core RPP specification.

section.name: Endpoints
section.t: The base_url element of the RPP Discovery response may include a version segment indicating the version of the RPP API supported by the server. A server MAY publish a base_url such as https://rpp.example/rpp/v1/ (the rpp.example authority and /rpp/v1 prefix being illustrative only).

section.name: Messages
section.t: The version element of the RPP request and response messages MUST include the version of the RPP API that the message is compatible with. The server MUST reject requests with a version that is not supported by the server, and MUST return an RPP Client error code.

section.name: Extensions
section.t: The RPP server MUST include all supported extensions and the version for each extension in the RPP Discovery response. The client MUST use this version information to determine which extensions are supported by the server, and to ensure that it uses the correct version of the extension when making requests to the server. The server MUST reject requests requiring extensions or unsupported versions of an extension that are not supported by the server. The set of extensions required by the client MUST be signalled by the client by using the correct profile, see .

section.name: Profiles
section.t: The RPP server MUST provide the set of supported profiles in the RPP Discovery response in the profiles element. The client can then request the appropriate profile from the server, using the profiles endpoint. The client MUST use this version information to determine which profiles are supported by the server, and to ensure that it uses the correct version of the profile when making requests to the server. A request using a profile MUST include the version of the profile. The server MUST reject requests using profiles with a version that is not supported by the server, and MUST return an RPP Client error code.

section.name: Media Types
section.t: RPP data can be transmitted using different representation formats, for example JSON or YAML. This document does not define a representation. Each representation is defined in a separate specification that registers an RPP media type for that representation, for example application/rpp+json. Each such specification also documents the security considerations of its underlying data format. Every RPP media type MUST support the profile and profile-version parameters defined in , so that profile signalling is identical for all representations.
An RPP client and an RPP server indicate and negotiate the media type of a message using the Content-Type () and Accept () header fields, as follows.
Requests:

ul.li: An RPP client MUST include an Accept header field in every request, including requests without content. Each media range in the Accept header field MUST identify an RPP media type the client is able to process in the response. The client MAY list more than one media range and MAY use quality values to indicate preference.
An RPP client sending a request MUST include a Content-Type header field identifying the requested RPP media type, even when there is no content.
The media type indicated in the Content-Type header field MUST also be acceptable according to the Accept header field of the same request.

section.t: Server processing:

ul.li: The RPP server MUST determine the data format of request content only from the Content-Type header field and MUST NOT infer it from the content. If the content does not conform to the data format of the indicated media type, the server MUST reject the request with the 400 (Bad Request) status code.
If the server does not support the media type indicated in the Content-Type header field, the server MUST reject the request with the 415 (Unsupported Media Type) status code.

The RPP server MUST select the media type for the response from the Accept header field using proactive negotiation as described in . If the server supports none of the listed media types, the server MUST reject the request with the 406 (Not Acceptable) status code.
If the media type indicated in the Content-Type header field is not acceptable according to the Accept header field, the server MUST reject the request with the 400 (Bad Request) status code.
In all rejection cases above, the server MUST include the RPP-Code header field and a Problem Detail response as described in .

section.t: Responses:

ul.li: An RPP server MUST include a Content-Type header field in every successful response. The media type MUST be one listed in the Accept header field of the request.
Problem Detail responses use the application/problem+json media type .
An RPP server MUST include Accept in the Vary header field of every response whose content depends on the negotiated media type or profile.

An RPP server SHOULD include the X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff header field in every response. Omitting it allows a browser-based RPP client to interpret a response as a media type other than the one indicated in Content-Type, which can expose registration data to scripts from another origin.

section.t: Client processing:

ul.li: The RPP client MUST determine the data format of response content only from the Content-Type header field and MUST NOT infer it from the content.

Except for Problem Detail responses, if the media type of a response was not listed in the Accept header field of the request, the client MUST NOT process the content as an RPP response and MUST treat the response as a protocol error.

section.name: Profile Signalling
section.t: This document describes two distinct methods for signalling the profile used in an RPP request or response, the first method uses a dedicated HTTP header field, the second method uses media type parameters. The two methods MUST NOT be used simultaneously in a single request or response. If both methods are used in a single request or response, then the server MUST return an HTTP error response and include a Problem Detail response in the content.

section.name: Rationale for Header Field Signalling
section.t: This section is not normative. Signalling the profile using a dedicated HTTP header field is preferable to signalling it using media type parameters, for the following reasons:

ul.li: Protocol level versus content level: the profile, and the RPP version it implies, determines how the whole HTTP message is interpreted, including URL paths, query parameters, and HTTP header fields, which can all evolve over time and need agreement between client and server. A media type only describes the format of the content. Signalling at the protocol level, in a header field, fits this scope better than signalling in a property of the content.

Independence of the representation format: media type parameters have to be mandated for, and implemented identically in, every RPP media type registered for every representation format. A header field is independent of the representation format, so a new representation format does not need to define any profile signalling and the profile signalling does not need to be changed when the media type handling changes.

Messages without content: Content-Type is only meaningful for a message that has content. Requests such as GET and DELETE, and responses without content, would otherwise have to carry a Content-Type header field only to signal the profile. A header field defined by RPP can be present in every request and response.
Separation of concerns: with a dedicated header field, media types are used only to negotiate the data format of the content, and the profile is negotiated independently of it.

aside.t: TODO: the working group has not yet decided on the signalling method to use, the two methods are both described until that decision is made.

section.name: Header Signalling
section.t: The client MUST use the RPP-Profile header field to indicate the name of the profile that is to be used for the request. The value of this header field is a Dictionary as defined in . The Dictionary MUST contain a profile member whose value uniquely identifies a profile, for example urn:ietf:params:rpp:profile:example-profile, and this member MUST carry a version parameter indicating the version of the profile. If the server does not support the indicated profile or version, then the server MUST return an HTTP error response and include a Problem Detail response in the content.
The ABNF for the RPP-Profile header field value is as follows:
section.sourcecode: profile-header = "profile" "=" profile-name ";" OWS "version" "=" version profile-name = token version = 1*DIGIT "." 1*DIGIT
section.t: Example:
section.sourcecode: GET /domainNames/foo.example HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json RPP-Profile: profile=urn:ietf:params:rpp:profile:example-profile;version=1.0 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345

section.name: Media Type Signalling
section.t: An RPP client and an RPP server select the profile that applies to a message using the media type parameters defined in this section, on top of the Content-Type and Accept header field handling defined in . The profiles supported by an RPP server are announced in the RPP Discovery document (see ).
The media type parameters are defined as follows:

ul.li: profile: The value of this parameter MUST uniquely identify the profile, for example urn:ietf:params:rpp:profile:example-profile.
profile-version: The value of this parameter MUST indicate the version of the profile.

section.t: The ABNF for the media type parameters is as follows:
section.sourcecode: profile-parameter = "profile" "=" profile-name ";" OWS "profile-version" "=" version profile-name = token version = 1*DIGIT "." 1*DIGIT
section.t: Requests:

ul.li: Each media range in the Accept header field of a request MUST include the profile and profile-version parameters of a profile the client is able to process in the response. The client MAY list more than one profile and MAY use quality values to indicate preference.
The media type in the Content-Type header field of a request with content MUST include the profile and profile-version parameters of the profile that the content conforms to.
The profile indicated in the Content-Type header field MUST also be listed in the Accept header field of the same request.

section.t: Server processing:

ul.li: The RPP server MUST determine the profile of request content only from the Content-Type header field and MUST NOT infer it from the content, and MUST process the content according to that profile.
If the server does not support the indicated profile or profile version, the server MUST reject the request with HTTP status code 415 (Unsupported Media Type).

The RPP server MUST select the profile for the response from the Accept header field using proactive negotiation as described in . If the server supports none of the listed profiles, the server MUST reject the request with HTTP status code 406 (Not Acceptable).
If the profile in the Content-Type header field is not listed in the Accept header field, the server MUST reject the request with HTTP status code 400 (Bad Request).
If a request does not include profile parameters, the server MUST apply the default profile advertised in the RPP Discovery document (see ).
The requested profile may include extensions that include additional HTTP header fields or query parameters that the server needs to understand and process correctly.
In all rejection cases above, the server MUST include the RPP-Code header field and a Problem Detail response as described in .

section.t: Responses:

ul.li: The media type in the Content-Type header field of a successful response that contains content MUST include the profile and profile-version parameters of the profile the server applied, and that profile MUST be one listed in the Accept header field of the request.
Problem Detail responses do not carry profile parameters.

section.t: Client processing:

ul.li: The RPP client MUST determine the profile of response content only from the Content-Type header field and MUST interpret the content according to that profile.

If that profile or profile version was not listed in the Accept header field of the request, the client MUST NOT process the content as an RPP response and MUST treat the response as a protocol error.
The requested profile may include extensions that include additional HTTP header fields or query parameters that the client needs to understand and process correctly.

section.t: Example of a request and the corresponding response header fields, using application/rpp+json for illustration:
section.sourcecode:
GET /domainNames/foo.example HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json; profile="urn:ietf:params:rpp:profile:example-profile"; profile-version="1.0" RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/rpp+json; profile="urn:ietf:params:rpp:profile:example-profile"; profile-version="1.0" Vary: Accept RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Process Signalling
section.t: When a server creates a process resource as a side effect of a uniform interface operation, it signals this to the client using the Link response header field with rel="rpp-process". The following target attributes are defined for this relation type:

ul.li: process: (REQUIRED) The process object identifier of the created process (e.g. process="transferProcess").

processId: (OPTIONAL) The server-assigned persistent identifier of the created process instance (e.g. processId="XYZ-12345"). If the server assigns a persistent identifier, this attribute MUST be included.

latest: (OPTIONAL) The boolean value true, indicating that the target URL is the latest process created of a given type. The target URL MAY use the latest mnemonic rather than a specific process identifier. There MUST NOT be more than one process of a given type with this attribute set to true.

section.t: If multiple process objects are created, the server MUST include one Link header field per created process resource.
Example:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Link: <https://rpp.example/rpp/domainNames/foo.example/processes/\ transferProcesses/XYZ-12345>; rel="rpp-process"; \ process="transferProcess"; processId="XYZ-12345"; latest="true" RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Endpoints
section.t: Endpoints are described using URI Templates relative to a discoverable base URL. The base URL, including its authority and any path prefix, is not defined by this specification; it is deployment-defined and discoverable by the client using the base_url field of the well-known discovery document, as described in . The URL paths used in the rules and examples below (e.g. /{collection}/{id}) are relative to the discovered base URL; the rpp.example authority and /rpp path prefix used in examples throughout this document are illustrative only and carry no normative meaning.

section.name: HTTP Mapping Rules
section.t: All RPP endpoints are derived mechanically from the Data Object definitions in . No endpoint URL or HTTP method related to processing of provisioning objects is defined independently of a corresponding Data Object. The rules in this section MUST be applied to determine the URL path and HTTP method for any operation.

section.name: Rule 1: Collection Path Segment
section.t: Each Data Object has a stable, Identifier (e.g. domainName, contact, host). The URL path segment for a collection of such objects MUST be derived by applying the plural() function to the object's Identifier. The plural() function appends an "s" or "es" to the identifier as per English language rules. Any irregular plural version MUST be defined in the data object specification.
Examples derived from current data object identifiers:

section.name: Rule 2: Uniform Interface Operations
section.t: The uniform interface operations defined in the RPP data object specification map to HTTP methods and URL paths as follows. {collection} is derived per Rule 1. {id} is the unique identifier value of the specific object instance.

section.name: Rule 3: Direct Access Sub-Resource Path Segment
section.t: A data element whose Direct Access flag is set to true in its Data Object definition is additionally exposed as a sub-resource, nested under the URL of the resource instance that contains it. This rule applies uniformly and recursively: the containing resource instance MAY itself be a Direct Access sub-resource of a further-enclosing resource.
The fixed path segment for such a sub-resource MUST be derived from the Direct Access data element's own Identifier — not from the Identifier of the associated object type the element references.

If the Direct Access element's cardinality is 0-1 or 1, the element's own Identifier MUST be used as the path segment, unpluralised; the resulting path already addresses a single instance unambiguously.

If the Direct Access element's cardinality is greater than 1, the plural() function MUST be applied to the element's Identifier to derive the path segment, and an individual associated object instance MUST be additionally addressed by appending its Unique Identifier value as a further path segment, {unique-id}. requires that any object type referenced by a Direct Access element of cardinality greater than 1 define a Unique Identifier for exactly this purpose.

Applying Rule 3 recursively from the top-level Data Object down to every Direct Access element defined in yields the following paths ({id} denotes the Unique Identifier value of the resource instance immediately to its left; it is instantiated per resource type as shown in the Derived Endpoint Reference below):

{collection} in the last four rows is derived per Rule 1 and stands for any owner Data Object's collection segment (e.g. domainNames, contacts); the Processes element and its nested Process Object elements are defined once, generically, and Direct Access sub-resources derive identically regardless of the owner Data Object type. {process-id} is the Process Object's Unique Identifier value; Rule 4 defines the latest mnemonic as an additional way to address it.
The remaining rules in this section (Rules 4 through 6) apply Rule 3 specifically to Process Objects and describe how they are further exposed and interacted with.

section.name: Rule 4: Process Uniform Interface Operations
section.t: The four uniform interface operations from Rule 2 apply to Process Objects at the path derived per Rule 3. A server MAY assign a unique identifier {process-id} to each process instance and make it addressable by this identifier. The fixed keyword latest is used to address the most recent process instance when no specific process {process-id} is known or assigned.

A started process MAY create a resource accessible using both the latest mnemonic and a server-assigned {process-id}. If the server exposes any access to a process instance, access to the most recent instance via latest MUST be supported.
When a process is created and immediately completed by the server, a 201 Created response MAY still be provided with a Location header field pointing to the created process resource.
If the server chooses not to expose any persistent process resource, it MUST return 200 OK instead of 201 Created.

The operations using the DELETE method MUST NOT accept request content, because the semantics of content in a DELETE request are not defined and may cause deployment issues. If request content is present for any operation using the DELETE method, the server MUST reject the request with an appropriate error response.

This means that the delete operation (HTTP DELETE method) is not extensible, if the server needs to support additional data for a special delete operation, then a new process MUST be defined for this purpose.

section.name: Rule 5: Extended Process Operations
section.t: Operations on a Process Object beyond the uniform interface (e.g. transferApprove, transferReject, report) are mapped to sub-resources of a specific process instance. The operation's Identifier is used unchanged as the final path segment. The HTTP method for all such extended operations MUST be POST.
The operation Identifier MUST be used as-is with no transformation. The following examples are derived directly from the operation identifiers defined in the RPP data object specification:

section.name: Rule 6: Process Listing
section.t: A server MAY implement a listing facility for processes. If implemented, the following URL structures MUST be used by the client.
To retrieve all process instances of a given process type:
To retrieve all process instances across all process types for an object:
A server MAY choose not to implement these endpoints, in which case it MUST return 404 Not Found or 501 Not Implemented.

section.name: Rule 7: Operation Parameters
section.t: An operation parameter defined in , such as includeElements MUST be included in the query component of the request URL, for every HTTP method, and MUST NOT be carried in the request content. This rule also applies to operation parameters added to an operation by an extension.
The query component is derived as follows:

ul.li: The parameter name MUST be the Identifier of the operation parameter, unchanged.
The parameter value MUST be the value of the data element, serialised as defined for its Data Type, only primitive types SHOULD be used.
An operation parameter with a cardinality of 0+ or 1+ MUST be repeated in the query component, once for each value.
Multiple operation parameters are allowed, no specific ordering is required.

section.t: Example request for a domain name, using the includeElements operation parameter to request an additional data element:
section.sourcecode: GET /domainNames/foo.example?includeElements=authInfo HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
section.t: The server MUST reject the request with the 400 (Bad Request) status code, the RPP-Code header field, and a Problem Detail response as described in if:

ul.li: The query component contains a parameter name that is not an operation parameter of the requested operation or of a supported extension;
A parameter with a cardinality of 0-1 or 1 occurs more than once;
A parameter value does not conform to the Data Type of the operation parameter.

section.name: Internationalized Domain Names (IDN)
section.t: When an Internationalized Domain Name (IDN) is used to identify a Domain Name Data Object or Host Data Object instance in a URL, in particular as the {id} path segment described in Rule 2, the ASCII Compatible Encoding (ACE) A-label form of the name, as defined in , MUST be used. This requirement ensures that the resulting URL remains a valid URI as defined in , since the A-label form is composed exclusively of ASCII characters and therefore requires no percent-encoding or additional Unicode normalisation when used as a URL path segment.

The Unicode (U-label) form of an internationalized name MUST NOT be used to address a resource in a URL. A client MAY submit or receive the U-label form as a separate data element as part of a resource representation, but this Unicode representation of the name as a whole MUST NOT be used when constructing or matching a URL.

This is consistent with the use of IDN in the DNS, the actual DNS name is naturally represented using its A-label form. This also avoids ambiguity: the URL identifies the DNS domain name rather than a particular Unicode representation of it.
For example, to address the domain name whose U-label is bücher.example, a client MUST use the corresponding A-label, xn--bcher-kva.example, when constructing the {id} path segment:
section.sourcecode: GET /domainNames/xn--bcher-kva.example HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345

section.name: Availability for Creation
section.t: The Availability for Creation endpoint maps the Availability operation defined in and is used to check whether an object can be successfully provisioned. Two distinct methods are defined for checking the availability of provisioning of an object, the first method uses the HEAD method for a quick check to find out if the object can be provisioned. The second method uses the GET method to retrieve the Availability Object, which may contain additional information, for example about pricing or additional requirements to be able to provision the requested object.

When the client uses the HTTP HEAD method, the server MUST respond with an HTTP status code 200 (OK) if the object can be provisioned or with an HTTP status code 404 (Not Found) if the object cannot be provisioned.

When the client uses the HTTP GET method, the server MUST respond with an HTTP status code 200 (OK) if the object can be provisioned. The server MUST include the Availability Object in the response content.
If the object cannot be provisioned then the server MUST return an HTTP status code 404 (Not Found) and include the Availability Object in the response content.
Parameters added to the Availability operation by extensions, for example to request a certain currency as defined in the Registry Fee Extension , are mapped to query parameters as described in .
The server MUST respond with the same HTTP status code if the same URL is requested with HEAD and with GET.
section.artwork: - Request: HEAD|GET /{collection}/{id}/availability - Request message: None - Response message: Availability Object (GET only)
section.t: Example request for a domain name that is not available for provisioning:
section.sourcecode: HEAD /domainNames/foo.example/availability HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Accept: application/rpp+json Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
section.t: Example response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Code: 01000 Content-Length: 0
section.t: Example request for an internationalized domain name, using the uName and lgr operation parameters to have the availability determined for the Unicode Name bücher.example against a specific LGR:
section.sourcecode: GET /domainNames/xn--bcher-kva.example/availability?\ uName=b%C3%BCcher.example&lgr=example-latn-1.0 HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
section.t: Example response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Type: application/rpp+json Content-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Code: 01000 Content-Length: 42

section.name: Resource Information
section.t: The Object Info request MUST use the HTTP GET method on a resource identifying an object instance (Rule 2, read operation). If the object has authorisation information attached then the client MUST send no content and include the RPP-Authorization header field. If the authorisation is linked to a database object the client MUST also include the roid in the RPP-Authorization header field. The client MAY also send content that includes the authorisation information, the client MUST then not use the RPP-Authorization header field.
Example request for an object not using authorisation information, using the hostsFilter operation parameter to only return delegated hosts:
section.sourcecode: GET /domainNames/foo.example?hostsFilter=del HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
section.t: Example request using the RPP-Authorization header field for an object that has attached authorisation information:
section.sourcecode: GET /domainNames/foo.example HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Authorization: authinfo value=TXkgU2VjcmV0IFRva2Vu
section.t: Example Info response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Length: 424 Content-Type: application/rpp+json Content-Language: en RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Create Resource
section.t: The client MUST use the HTTP POST method on a resource identifying a collection of object instances (Rule 2, create operation).
Example Domain Create request for a new domain name foo.example:
section.sourcecode:
POST /domainNames HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Content-Type: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Content-Length: 220

section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Language: en Content-Length: 642 Content-Type: application/rpp+json Location: https://rpp.example/rpp/domainNames/foo.example RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000
section.t: Example Domain Create response where a createProcess object was implicitly created:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Language: en Content-Type: application/rpp+json Location: https://rpp.example/rpp/domainNames/foo.example Link: <https://rpp.example/rpp/domainNames/foo.example/processes/createProcesses/latest>; rel="rpp-process"; process="createProcess"; processId="XYZ-12345" RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Delete Resource
section.t: The client MUST use the HTTP DELETE method on a resource identifying a unique object instance (Rule 2, delete operation).
Example Domain Delete request:
section.sourcecode: DELETE /domainNames/foo.example HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
section.t: Example Domain Delete response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Length: 80 Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Update Resource
section.t: RPP supports two complementary update operations for modifying an existing object instance, each with its own semantics and use cases:

li.t: Full update (HTTP PUT): The client sends a complete replacement representation of the object. The server MUST replace the stored object with the provided representation. Any attributes not present in the request content MUST be treated as absent and cleared or reset to their default values, subject to server policy. The client MUST send all read-write attributes required by the data model, not just the changed ones. The client MUST NOT send any create-only attributes.

Partial update (HTTP PATCH): The client sends only the attributes to be modified. The server MUST apply only the changes indicated in the request content and leave all other attributes unchanged. Data representation of the partial update payload determines how the changes are transmitted between client and server and applied to the data object. The client MAY send changes to any read-write attributes defined in the data model. The client MUST NOT send any create-only attributes.

section.t: Both operations MUST be performed on a URL identifying a unique object instance (Rule 2). The request content MUST contain a valid object representation in the negotiated media type.
The server MUST respond with HTTP status code 200 (OK) and include the updated object representation in the response content.
Example full update request (PUT):
section.sourcecode: PUT /domainNames/foo.example HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Content-Type: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Content-Length: 252
section.t: Example full update response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Length: 80 Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000
section.t: Example partial update request (PATCH):
section.sourcecode: PATCH /domainNames/foo.example HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Content-Type: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Content-Length: 252
section.t: Example partial update response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Length: 80 Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Processes
section.t: Each provisioning object may be related to one or more running processes, such as a transfer or renewal. Each process has its own data, distinct from the data of the provisioning object itself, and may be interacted with using its own set of operations.
All process resources MUST exist under the /{collection}/{id}/processes/{process-collection} path, where {process-collection} is derived per Rule 3.

section.name: Relation to Object Representation
section.t: A uniform interface operation MAY require process data in addition to the object representation data. How the process data is embedded in the request content MUST be defined in the corresponding representation specification.

section.name: Response with Information about Created Process
section.t: When the server creates a process object as a side effect of the operation, it MUST signal this to the client as described in .

section.name: Restore Resource
section.t: The Restore operation manages the recovery of an object that has entered the Redemption Grace Period (RGP) . Restore is modelled as a Process Object with its own lifecycle. The restoreProcess object identifier yields the restoreProcesses collection segment per Rule 3.

The client MUST use the HTTP POST method to create a new restore process (Rule 4, create). The server MUST reject the request with HTTP status code 409 (Conflict) and RPP result code 02304 if the object is not in the rgpRedemptionPeriod state. If the server exposes the created restore process resource (see Rule 4), the response MUST include the Location header field for that resource.
Example Domain Restore request:
section.sourcecode: POST /domainNames/foo.example/processes/restoreProcesses HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Accept-Language: en Content-Length: 96
section.t: Example Restore response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Language: en RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Content-Length: 85 Location: https://rpp.example/rpp/domainNames/foo.example/processes/restoreProcesses/XYZ-12345 Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Code: 01000
section.t: To submit a restore report for an object in the rgpPendingRestore state, the client MUST use the HTTP PUT or PATCH method to update the restore process (Rule 4, update). The server MUST reject the request with HTTP status code 409 (Conflict) and RPP result code 02304 if the object is not in the rgpPendingRestore state.
Example Domain Restore Report request:
section.sourcecode: PUT /domainNames/foo.example/processes/restoreProcesses/latest HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12346 Accept-Language: en Content-Length: 180
section.t: To retrieve the current state of the restore process, the client MUST use the HTTP GET method (Rule 4, read) and MUST NOT send content in the request.

section.name: Renew Resource
section.t: Renew is modelled as a Process Object with its own lifecycle. The renewProcess object identifier yields the renewProcesses collection segment per Rule 3.
The client MUST use the HTTP POST method to create a new renew process (Rule 4, create).

Not every object resource includes support for the renew command. If the server exposes the created renew process resource (see Rule 4), the response MUST include the Location header field for that resource.
Example Domain Renew request:
section.sourcecode: POST /domainNames/foo.example/processes/renewProcesses HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Accept-Language: en Content-Length: 96
section.t: Example Renew response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Language: en RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Content-Length: 85 Location: https://rpp.example/rpp/domainNames/foo.example/processes/renewProcesses/XYZ-12345 Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Transfer Resource
section.t: The Transfer operation manages the change of sponsoring client for a provisioned object. Transfer is modelled as a Process Object with its own lifecycle. The transferProcess object identifier yields the transferProcesses collection segment per Rule 3.

section.name: Start
section.t: The initiating client MUST use the HTTP POST method to create a new transfer process (Rule 4, create).
Example request not using object authorisation:
section.sourcecode: POST /domainNames/foo.example/processes/transferProcesses HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Content-Type: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Content-Length: 320
section.t: Example request using object authorisation:
section.sourcecode: POST /domainNames/foo.example/processes/transferProcesses HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Authorization: authinfo value=TXkgU2VjcmV0IFRva2Vu Accept-Language: en Content-Length: 320
section.t: Example Transfer response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 201 Created Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Language: en Content-Length: 182 Content-Type: application/rpp+json Location: https://rpp.example/rpp/domainNames/foo.example/processes/transferProcesses/latest RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01001

section.name: Status
section.t: A transfer process resource may not exist when no transfer has been initiated for the specified object. The client MUST use the HTTP GET method and MUST NOT send content in the request.
Example domain name Transfer Status request:
section.sourcecode: GET /domainNames/foo.example/processes/transferProcesses/latest HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
section.t: Example Transfer Status response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Length: 230 Content-Type: application/rpp+json Content-Language: en RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Cancel
section.t: The initiating client cancels its pending transfer request using the DELETE method on the process resource (Rule 4, delete).
Example request:
section.sourcecode: DELETE /domainNames/foo.example/processes/transferProcesses/latest HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
section.t: Example response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Length: 80 Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Reject
section.t: The currently sponsoring client rejects a pending transfer. This is an extended process operation; the operation identifier transferReject is used unchanged as the final path segment (Rule 5).
Example request:
section.sourcecode: POST /domainNames/foo.example/processes/transferProcesses/latest/transferReject HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Content-Length: 0
section.t: Example response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Length: 80 Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Approve
section.t: The currently sponsoring client approves a pending transfer. The operation identifier transferApprove is used unchanged as the final path segment (Rule 5).
Example request:
section.sourcecode: POST /domainNames/foo.example/processes/transferProcesses/latest/transferApprove HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Content-Length: 0
section.t: Example response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Length: 80 Content-Type: application/rpp+json RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01000

section.name: Messages
section.t: The messages endpoint exposes a server-side durable queue of asynchronous notifications generated for a client, for example to report the completion of an operation that was processed out-of-band, such as a Transfer request requiring approval from another party. The server MUST retain a message in the queue until it has been explicitly acknowledged by the client. Retrieval and acknowledgement of a message are deliberately separate operations, using a separate resource and HTTP method for each: the client uses the HTTP GET method to retrieve one or more messages, and the HTTP DELETE method, addressed at a specific message, to acknowledge it. A message that is retrieved but never acknowledged MUST remain in the queue and MUST be made available for redelivery, as described below, so that every message is guaranteed to eventually be delivered to, and can be processed by, the client, subject to the server-initiated deletion described below.

Each message is linked to a single organisation. Only the organisation to which a message is linked is permitted to retrieve or acknowledge that message; the server MUST NOT return a message to, or accept an acknowledgement of a message from, any other organisation.

Notwithstanding the guarantees described in this section, the server MAY delete a message from the queue at any time, including before it has been acknowledged, for example to enforce a retention policy or reclaim storage. Deletion of unacknowledged messages is therefore a best-effort guarantee and clients SHOULD NOT rely on the eventual delivery of every message for correctness.

The server MAY include the RPP-Queue-Size header field (see ) in any RPP response, not only in responses to Messages requests, to inform the client of the current number of unacknowledged messages in its queue without requiring a dedicated Retrieve request.

Each message follows a lifecycle, as depicted in below, and has a status of either queued, delivered or removed. A message is queued from the moment it is created until it is returned to a client in a Retrieve response, at which point its status changes to delivered. The server MUST associate an acknowledge timeout (i.e., the maximum time the client has to acknowledge the message) with a message when its status changes to delivered. If the client does not acknowledge the message before this timeout elapses, the server MUST revert its status back to queued, making it available again for retrieval, including by a different client or reader, as a retry mechanism for a client that crashed or otherwise failed to acknowledge the message. Because of this retry mechanism, a message may be delivered more than once and client message processing MUST be idempotent. Choosing an appropriate delivery timeout duration is an implementation and deployment decision and is out of scope for this document.

The following diagram illustrates the message state transitions described above, including the deletion of a message by the client or server which is permitted while the message is in either the queued or the delivered state:

The server MAY support multiple simultaneous readers concurrently retrieving messages from the same queue, for example multiple worker processes operated by the same client. The server MUST NOT return the same queued message to more than one Retrieve request at a time; once a message has been returned to a reader and its status changes to delivered, it MUST NOT be returned again to any reader until its delivery timeout has elapsed and its status has reverted to queued.

The server MUST return queued messages in the order in which they were inserted into the queue, so that the oldest queued message is always the next one returned to a Retrieve request. A message that reverts from delivered back to queued after its delivery timeout has elapsed MUST be treated, for ordering purposes, according to its original insertion order rather than being moved to the end of the queue.

section.name: Retrieve
section.t: The messages endpoint is used for retrieving exactly one message stored on the server for the client to process. The client may use the following query parameter to control which messages are returned:

ul.li: type (OPTIONAL): Restricts the response to messages of the given message type. This parameter MAY be repeated to request messages of more than one type. If omitted, messages of any type MAY be returned.

section.t: Every message has a type, identifying the kind of notification it represents. When the client uses the type query parameter, only queued messages matching one of the requested types transition to delivered and are included in the response. A queued message that does not match the requested type MUST remain in the queue with a status of queued, even if it is ahead, per the ordering rules above, of a matching message that is returned; the type filter does not otherwise change the relative position of a message in the queue.

Query parameters are used here for simplicity. A future revision of this document may instead, or additionally, define an equivalent request format using the HTTP QUERY method , which would allow more expressive filtering to be conveyed in the request content rather than the request URL.

The server SHOULD return the human-readable content of a message in the language requested by the client's Accept-Language header field. Not every message type may support every language; if the requested language is not available for a given message, the server MUST fall back to returning that message in its own default language.
Every message returned in the response transitions from queued to delivered as described above.
In the EPP Compatibility Profile, the following limitations apply:

ul.li: The RPP server always returns the oldest message in the EPP poll queue.
Multiple sequential requests from the same client return the same message until the message is acknowledged.
The type query parameter is ignored. The server always returns the oldest message in the EPP poll queue, regardless of its type.

When multiple readers are used, each reader independently receives the oldest message in the EPP poll queue. Consequently, multiple readers may receive the same message, possibly multiple times, until that message is acknowledged.
The messages remain in the queued state.

section.t: Example request for retrieving a new message of the type transferRequestMessage only:
section.sourcecode: GET /messages?type=transferRequestMessage HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
section.t: Example response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 Content-Length: 312 Content-Type: application/rpp+json Content-Language: en RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 RPP-Code: 01301 RPP-Queue-Size: 4

section.name: Acknowledge
section.t: The client MUST use the HTTP DELETE method to acknowledge receipt of a single message from the queue. The id attribute of a received message MUST be included in the message resource URL, using the {id} path element. Once successfully acknowledged, the message MUST be permanently removed from the queue. The server MUST NOT send content in the response to a successful delete request. When the delete request fails for any reason, the server MUST include a Problem Detail document in the content of the error response.
Example request:
section.sourcecode: DELETE /messages/12345 HTTP/1.1 Host: rpp.example Authorization: Bearer <token> Accept: application/rpp+json Accept-Language: en RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345
section.t: Example response:
section.sourcecode: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Wed, 24 Jan 2024 12:00:00 GMT Server: Example RPP server v1.0 RPP-Code: 01000 RPP-Queue-Size: 0 RPP-Svtrid: XYZ-12345 RPP-Cltrid: ABC-12345 Content-Length: 0

section.name: Result Codes
section.t: RPP result codes are used to indicate the outcome of an RPP request, they are defined to be backwards compatible with the EPP result codes defined in and other EPP specifications and extensions.
Two distinct namespaces are defined for RPP result codes:

ul.li: Result codes derived from EPP and other EPP specifications and extensions, which use a leading digit of 0.
RPP-specific result codes, which use a leading digit of 1.

section.t: RPP result codes follow the theory of reply codes described in . An RPP result code consists of five decimal digits, each digit has a special significance:

ul.li: The first digit identifies the namespace, 1 for RPP-specific result codes.
The second digit denotes the success or failure of the request, see the classes of result codes below.
The third digit denotes the category of the result, such as syntax or security.
The fourth and fifth digits provide the explicit result detail within the category.

section.t: The second digit has two possible values:

ul.li: 1: Positive completion. The request was accepted and processed by the server without error.
2: Negative completion. The request was not accepted, and the requested action did not occur.

section.t: The third digit groups the results into one of six categories:

ul.li: 0: Protocol syntax
1: Implementation-specific rules
2: Security
3: Data management
4: Server system
5: Connection management

section.t: For example, the RPP result code 02303 is an EPP-derived (0) failure (2) in the data management category (3), with the detail "Object does not exist" (03).

Every RPP result code defined in this document and in future standardised RPP extensions MUST be registered with IANA to ensure uniqueness and avoid conflicts. An IANA registry for RPP result codes is defined in the IANA Considerations section.
Newly defined RPP result codes, for example in future extensions, MUST NOT use the namespace reserved for result codes derived from EPP.

section.name: Mapping RPP Result Codes to HTTP Status Codes
section.t: RPP result codes are mapped to HTTP status codes, allowing clients to handle responses using common HTTP patterns. The RPP result code, describing the specific outcome of an RPP process, MUST always be returned using the RPP-Code header field. This enables the client to take appropriate action based on the detailed result code.

The mapping strategy is to map an RPP result code to the most applicable HTTP status code, when no such mapping can be defined then the RPP result code MUST be mapped to a general HTTP status code (e.g. 200, 400, and 500).

The second and third digits of an RPP result code MUST be used to map the result code to a class of HTTP status codes, as defined in . The leading namespace digit and the last two detail digits do not influence the class.

section.name: Authentication and Authorisation
section.t: Due to the stateless nature of RPP, the client MUST include the authentication credentials in each HTTP request. This MAY be done by using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) or Basic authentication . The server MUST validate the authentication credentials on each request and reject any request with invalid credentials with an appropriate HTTP status code.

When using JWTs for OAuth 2.0 Access Tokens, the JWT profile described in MUST be used. It is RECOMMENDED to use short-lived tokens and to implement token revocation mechanisms to mitigate the risk of token compromise. If sensitive information is included in the JWT payload, it MUST be encrypted to prevent unauthorised access when the token is persisted to a storage device. Furthermore, the best practices for JWT usage as outlined in MUST be followed.

section.t: The IANA is requested to create a new registry "RPP Result codes", this registry will be used to register RPP result codes defined in this document and in future RPP specifications and extensions.

ul.li: code: The RPP result code, for example 01000.
origin: The origin of the result code, indicating whether it is derived from EPP or defined specifically for RPP.
description: A human-readable description of the result code and its intended use.

section.name: Link Relation Type
section.t: The IANA is requested to register the "rpp-process" link relation type in the "Link Relation Types" registry, following the template in :
section.sourcecode: Relation Name: rpp-process Description: Identifies a process resource that was implicitly created as a side effect of a uniform interface operation on the target resource. The context resource is the provisioning object on which the operation was performed; the target resource is the created process instance. The following target attributes are defined for this relation type: "process" (the Process Object Identifier, required), "processId" (the server-assigned process instance identifier, optional), and "latest" (the boolean value "true", optional, indicating the target URL uses the "latest" mnemonic). Reference: This document

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: RPP relies on the security of the underlying HTTP transport, hence the best common practices for securing HTTP described in also apply to RPP and MUST be followed by RPP implementations.

Data confidentiality and integrity MUST be enforced. Every client and server interaction MUST be encrypted using TLS version 1.3 . Future versions of TLS MAY be used as they become available and are deemed secure.

RPP does not mandate a single data format; media types for RPP messages can use JSON, YAML, or any other data format. Each RPP media type specification MUST document the security considerations applicable to its underlying format (e.g. for JSON), in addition to the considerations described in this section. An implementation that infers the data format or profile of a message from its content, rather than from the Content-Type header field, risks processing the message with the wrong parser or feature set; therefore requires both RPP clients and RPP servers to rely on the header field only.

An RPP client MUST verify the identity of the RPP server, as described in , before sending any request. The client MUST validate the TLS server certificate, including that the certificate chain is trusted and that the certificate matches the host name of the URL used to access the RPP server. If the validation fails, the client MUST NOT continue and MUST NOT send the request.
